newsitem.title: UK: U.K. petrol retailers say laws favour supermarkets.
newsitem.headline: U.K. petrol retailers say laws favour supermarkets.

text.p: Britain's largest supermarkets enjoy unfair advantages in the ferocious retail petrol market where the rate of site closures in 1996 was double that of 1995, the Petroleum Retailers Association (PRA) said.

Independent retailers were also vulnerable to discrimination and contractual abuse because the major oil companies did not operate under general codes of practice, the PRA, in evidence published on Monday, told a House of Commons trade and industry subcommittee.
Some independent retailers testified that up to 3,000 service stations could close in 1997, roughly the same number as last year.
The government estimated there were about 16,000 filling stations in Britain in 1996, against 22,000 in 1984.
The supermarkets are not required to meet certain stock holding requirements that refiners do, even though they operate under their own brands and are a major force in the market, PRA said.

"They enjoy a strategic stock advantage of 10 days over refiners which allows them to operate at lower cost than the oil company equivalent networks," PRA said. "This seems to be a hidden subsidy and distorts competition quite unnecessarily."
Supermarket chain Tesco Plc has a larger market share than any oil company other than Esso or Shell, with 10 percent, PRA, citing Esso, said.
J. Sainsbury Plc holds a market share of five percent, it said.

The trade group was refuting last summer's arguments from the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) and the government, when they rejected recommendations by the committee to alleviate the rapid rate of petrol site closings, mostly among independents.
The OFT and government were recalled in December after the committee felt its measures were not being taken seriously in the midst of a petrol price war.
The oil companies were accused of selling below cost to drive their competition out of business and eventually boost prices.
The price war was sparked a year ago when Esso, a unit of U.S. major Exxon Corp, launched its Pricewatch campaign that promised to match the lowest prices in its markets.

The government argued that it had not identified "any significant distortions to competition" and that retailers and refiners disagreed over which party "appears to be carrying a lower share of the burden."
The government agreed the closure rate would be higher in 1996 than 1995 and that some sites would be unable to compete with the supermarkets.
PRA also accused the OFT of lacking the resources to monitor the petrol industry, another committee recommendation.

"In the light of the very poor quality of the evidence of the OFT, and the total absence of any evidence of either the launch of Esso Pricewatch or its effect thereafter, we have concluded that the OFT scaled down its monitoring...to a level which might be described as perfunctory and dependent upon complaint and pump price checking," it said.

The committee had also recommended a code of practice be drawn up to cover the contractual relationships between wholesalers and retailers and include provisions for speedy and binding arbitration of disputes.
The OFT response to the committee that implied all oil companies operated general codes of practice was incorrect, PRA said.
The current codes apply only to licensees of oil company owned service stations, not to independent dealers, it said.
-- Mike Peacock/John Hanley, 44 171 542 8185
